text.p: Brain Warp, Tickle Me Elmo and Laser Challenger might be flying off retailers' shelves quicker than Santas can grab them, but the hottest product this Christmas is none of the above.
The best seller? The batteries that power them.
This year, as many as 4 billion batteries will be sold, fully 40 percent of them in the holiday season.
Consumers will snap up more batteries this year than ever before in a public hunger for newer, smaller and more portable electronic devices of all kinds.
All this has naturally ignited a heated marketing war among the three big players, Duracell, Panasonic and Energiser.
Each of the three rivals has boosted its ad budget this year and unleashed a steady stream of incentive promotions at the retail level.
While each uses saturation advertising on television to say its battery is better, a growing part of the game is pitching products where purchases are made -- the closer to the checkout, the better.

"At Duracell, we are generating as many as 1,000 promotions a month, customising them for specific retailers," reports Bob Giacolone, vice president for marketing at Duracell USA, in Bethel, Conn. "As a typical example, at the Stop & Shop supermarkets in New England, a shopper who buys two packages of batteries gets a free, two-litre bottle of soda."

Duracell also uses 30-second TV commercials developed by Ogilvy & Mather WPP Plc in New York. One portrays the evolution of the battery in a computer animation sequence directed by Roman Coppola, the son of the movie director, Francis Ford Coppola.

Duracell is the nation's largest battery maker but Panasonic claims to be the biggest producer internationally, running full-page advertisements in the trade press proclaiming, "Who Makes and Sells More Batteries Than Anyone Else in the World?" Answering itself, Panasonic said it manufactures and sells more batteries (in dollars) than any other company.

Battery makers felt competition heat up this year this year when Gillette Co. bought Duracell International for $7.1 billion. Its razorblades and toothbrushes dominate supermarket displays, and now brings its marketing power to the battery market.

"It probably will give Duracell more resources and may help get them more shelf space," conceded Todd Schrader, marketing manager for the Panasonic Sales Group, Secaucus, N.J. Schrader, though, says Panasonic is responding by planning "more sell-through promotions, such as deals on soda, school supplies, more coupons."
Panasonic is also pushing a high-capacity AA battery, and using the trade press to bring its message to retailers, using mostly advertising prepared by Grey Advertising New York.

The most visible advertiser is Energiser, produced by the Eveready Battery Co., St. Louis, which is heavily promoting its on-battery tester, with such ad banners as "Energizer has a GOOD thing going ... and going.. and going ...," and citing the green dot on the battery, which indicates the remaining life on the battery when pressed for five or 10 seconds.
